extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and attorneys who practice before the USPTO (and parties in USPTO disciplinary proceedings)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings evaluating practitioner conduct, service, burden of proof, and sanctions under 37 C.F.R. part 11 and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper service of complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2) and § 11.11 address)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must serve the complaint on the respondent pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2) by sending copies to the practitioner's address of record; 37 C.F.R. § 11.11 requires a registered practitioner to notify OED of the postal address for the practitioner's office and any change within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision describes mailing three certified copies to the practitioner's § 11.11 address and other known addresses; USPS delivery or signed certified-mail receipts are used to infer receipt. Notices mailed to the address of record are treated as proper service even if other addresses exist or mail is later forwarded or returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to answer complaint and consequence of failure (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal sets deadlines (Notice of Hearing and Order) and stays; failure to file an answer or to respond to a motion may result in drawing the permissible inference of receipt and entry of default judgment. Motions are subject to local response deadlines (e.g., opposition within ten days after docketing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged disciplinary violations by clear and convincing evidence; respondents likewise must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision quotes authorities explaining that clear and convincing proof lies between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt and requires evidence that produces a firm belief or conviction. Evidence must be certain, unambiguous, and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner "shall provide competent representation to a client."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence violations include filing applications improperly (e.g., incorrect micro-entity certification), failing to include required fees/surcharges, or otherwise performing tasks such that the client's application becomes abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner "shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violations are failing to respond to Office actions, restriction/election requirements, Ex parte Quayle actions, or Notices to File Missing Parts, causing abandonment of applications. Diligence includes timely filing replies or obtaining necessary extensions under 37 C.F.R. § 1.136(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the client's matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to notify clients of Office actions, Notices of Abandonment, or options to respond constitutes a violation. The decision cites multiple counts where clients were not informed of important Office communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly comply with reasonable client information requests (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonresponse to client emails and queries (e.g., status inquiries) is a violation; repeated failure to respond supports findings of intentional neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain matters sufficiently for informed client decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall "explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include not explaining the consequences of failing to respond to Office communications or failing to advise on options to revive or correct filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is proscribed to fail to cooperate with an OED investigation or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from a disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision details the mailing of Requests for Information (RFI) and Lack of Response letters and finds failure to respond (or request extensions) despite ample notice and receipt as a violation that also supports aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to "engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision finds misrepresentation where the practitioner asserted that no extension fee was due while the facts showed otherwise (e.g., paying the surcharge later), and notes that such behavior supports serious discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to "engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to cooperate in an investigation, ignoring disciplinary proceedings, and otherwise obstructing the disciplinary process undermines public trust and is treated as prejudicial conduct warranting aggravation of sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors to determine discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining an appropriate sanction the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors to weigh exclusion versus lesser sanctions. The existence of actual injury (e.g., abandonment causing lost patent life) and knowing/intentional conduct support more severe penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards § 9.22) used in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple violations; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders of OED; and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal cited these aggravators (dishonest motive, pattern across multiple clients/applications, multiple offenses, bad faith obstruction, substantial experience) as supporting the severe sanction of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA Standards § 9.32) used in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors may justify reduction in discipline; the decision notes one: the absence of a prior disciplinary record (Standards § 9.32(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision found limited weight in mitigation given the seriousness and pattern of misconduct; mitigating factors must be balanced against aggravators and injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is not to punish but to protect the public and the administration of justice from lawyers who have not discharged, will not discharge, or are unlikely properly to discharge their professional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle guides sanction selection (focus on protection and deterrence). The decision cites precedent applying the protective purpose to justify exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for reinstatement and responsibilities after exclusion (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.60(b), 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b)); practitioners should refer to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 for responsibilities in case of suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision orders exclusion and notifies the respondent of the five-year minimum before applying for reinstatement and of duties during suspension/exclusion (e.g., notice requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural handling of default motions and opportunity to resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: Before seeking default judgment, the OED Director may send a letter notifying the respondent of intent to file a default motion and invite contact to resolve the motion; motions are subject to oppositions and local timing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record shows counsel invited respondent to contact counsel before a deadline; the tribunal enforces response deadlines and treats lack of response as supporting default entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity certification and application-identifying requirements (MPEP 509.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Certification of Micro Entity Status must identify the application to which it pertains; for filings before an application number is assigned, the first named inventor and the correct title of the invention must be provided, and all identifying information must be consistent with the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inconsistent title on the certification prevents micro entity status and results in incorrect fee payments; the Office issues Notices to File Corrected Application Papers with a statutory period to correct and warns that failure may lead to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees, surcharges, and extensions for late replies (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.16(f), 1.136(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices indicate when surcharges (e.g., $35 under § 1.16(f)) are required for late submissions and that extensions of time may be available under § 1.136(a); failing to include requisite surcharge or extension fee can render a reply incomplete and lead to abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision recounts instances where a practitioner submitted a micro-entity certification but omitted the required $35 surcharge or the extension fee needed to make a late filing permissible, producing Notices of Incomplete Reply and eventual abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailing of Office communications to practitioner address of record and duty to monitor
rubrics_metrics.description: Office communications (Office actions, Notices to File Missing Parts, Ex parte Quayle actions, Notices of Abandonment) are mailed to the practitioner address designated in the application and to the practitioner’s address of record; practitioners have a duty to monitor mail and forward communications to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal treated mailings to the firm's business address and to addresses on record with OED/State Bar as effective; failure to receive or forward mail is not a defense where mail was sent to the designated address and certified receipts show delivery or authorized signature.
